blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The Authorization header, hence every bearer token, is written to the logs) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a hash of the token (e.g. SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes; a slow hash is not needed for high-entropy values) in a `token_hash` column and look requests up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` on the hash of the presented token — still a single indexed equality, so the lookup stays fast. Attack without it: anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table (a database backup, a read replica, a SQL injection elsewhere, an operator) gets bearer credentials usable as is against the API for every user, unlike `users.password_hash` which is bcrypt (CWE-312, CWE-256). Update tasks 1.1 and 1.2 accordingly, and drop "none, the lookup must be fast" from the alternatives, since hashing keeps it fast.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
To diagnose integration problems, the middleware logs each request's
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Never log `Authorization` (nor `Cookie` / `Set-Cookie`): redact it, or log a non-secret identifier instead — the token's row id or a short prefix / fingerprint of its hash — so support can still tell which token was sent. Attack without it: anyone with read access to the logs (support staff, a log aggregation service, a leaked log archive) collects working tokens and calls the API as their owners (CWE-532); it also defeats R-security-1, since the clear tokens end up in the logs even once the table is hashed. Task 1.3 ("Request logging in the middleware, verified by `cargo test logs_requests`") should assert that the header is absent from the log line.
findings.title: The Authorization header, hence every bearer token, is written to the logs

findings.recommendation: Either bring a minimal revocation (delete a token by id, owner-checked) into this change, or state in the proposal that it must not be released before the revocation change, and record that dependency. Attack without it: a token leaked from an integration (the very threat the proposal names: "a leaked integration exposes the account") stays valid indefinitely; the user cannot invalidate it, and unlike a password it is not changed by a password reset, so the attacker keeps full account access through the API. The Risks section only covers a lost token, not a leaked one.
findings.title: A leaked token cannot be revoked, so the change ships without a way to cut off a compromised integration
